Crystallization occurs when atoms arrange themselves into an ordered, repeating three-dimensional pattern—a crystal lattice. Once this initial nucleus had formed, other silicon and oxygen atoms in the surrounding magma were attracted to it. ## Part Two: Geological Transformation (300 Million to 2 Million Years Ago)

### The Permian Period: Grain X Enters the Sedimentary System

As we enter the Permian period, approximately 300 million years ago, Grain X's history takes a significant turn. No longer is it a component of the crystalline granite from which it originated. Instead, it has become a loose mineral grain, part of the sedimentary system that characterizes the Earth's surface. This transition marks a fundamental change in Grain X's existence—from a stable, unchanging crystal buried deep within the Earth to a mobile particle subject to the forces of erosion, transport, and deposition.

At this time, Grain X was located in a river system that flowed across a vast continental landscape. The region in which Grain X was located was in the interior of this supercontinent, far from any ocean. The climate was warm and dry, with seasonal rainfall. The crystal, which had originally had a relatively angular shape with sharp faces, gradually became more rounded.

This process of abrasion is one of the most important processes in the formation of sand grains. As a mineral grain is transported by water, it collides with other grains and with rocks on the river bed. Each collision removes a tiny amount of material from the grain's surface. Over thousands of collisions, the cumulative effect is significant. The grain becomes progressively smaller and more rounded.

Grain X's composition—quartz—made it particularly resistant to abrasion. Quartz is one of the hardest minerals found in nature, with a hardness of 7 on the Mohs hardness scale. This means that quartz grains are not easily abraded by collisions with other quartz grains or with rocks composed of softer minerals. However, quartz grains can be abraded by collisions with other quartz grains and with rocks composed of harder minerals, such as diamond or corundum. In the river system where Grain X was located, there were no diamonds or corundum, so the abrasion of Grain X was relatively slow.

Over the course of several million years, Grain X was reduced in size from approximately 2 millimeters in diameter to approximately 1 millimeter in diameter. ### The Permian-Triassic Boundary and Environmental Change

Approximately 252 million years ago, a catastrophic event occurred that would have profound effects on the Earth's geology and biology. Approximately 96% of all marine species and 70% of all terrestrial vertebrate species went extinct during this event.

The causes of this extinction event are still debated by scientists, but the most widely accepted explanation involves a combination of factors. The warming of the oceans caused them to become anoxic—devoid of dissolved oxygen—which killed most marine life. The warming also disrupted the hydrological cycle, causing droughts in some regions and floods in others.

For Grain X, the Permian-Triassic extinction event had indirect effects. The vegetation that covered the landscape was devastated by the environmental changes. Many plant species went extinct. The forests that had covered the landscape were replaced by sparse vegetation adapted to the harsh conditions. This change in vegetation affected the rate of erosion and weathering. With less vegetation to hold the soil in place, erosion rates increased. More sediment was washed into the rivers, and the rivers became more turbulent and fast-flowing.

Grain X was caught up in this increased sediment transport. It was moved downstream more rapidly than before, traveling greater distances in shorter periods of time. The increased turbulence of the rivers meant that Grain X collided with other grains more frequently, and it was abraded more rapidly.

### The Jurassic Period: Deposition in a Coastal Environment

By approximately 200 million years ago, Grain X had reached the coast. The river in which it had been traveling for millions of years had finally reached the ocean. Grain X was now in a coastal environment, where rivers met the sea.

Grain X, being relatively heavy, settled quickly. It came to rest on the ocean floor, in a shallow marine environment, surrounded by other mineral grains, shells, and organic matter.

The ocean floor in this region was not static. Waves and tidal currents stirred up the sediment, moving it back and forth. Grain X would be picked up by the currents and transported a short distance, then deposited again. ### Burial and Compaction

Over the course of millions of years, Grain X was buried beneath layers of sediment. New sediment was constantly being deposited on top of it, as rivers continued to transport sediment to the coast and as shells and other organic matter accumulated on the ocean floor. As the sediment accumulated, the pressure on Grain X increased. The grains were pressed together more tightly, and the spaces between them—the pores—were reduced. This process is called compaction. The sediment was gradually being converted into sedimentary rock.

Grain X was now part of a sandstone—a sedimentary rock composed primarily of sand-sized mineral grains. The sandstone was being buried deeper and deeper, as more and more sediment accumulated on top of it. The temperature increased as Grain X was buried deeper. At a depth of 1 kilometer, the temperature was approximately 40 to 50 degrees Celsius. At a depth of 2 kilometers, the temperature was approximately 60 to 70 degrees Celsius.

### Cementation and Lithification

As the sandstone was buried deeper, another process began to occur. Water that was trapped in the pores between the grains began to dissolve minerals from the surrounding rock. This mineral-rich water flowed through the pores and deposited minerals on the surfaces of the grains. Over time, these minerals accumulated and formed a cement that bound the grains together. This process is called cementation, and it is the final step in the conversion of sediment into sedimentary rock.

The cement that bound Grain X to its neighbors was composed primarily of quartz and calcite. Calcite cement formed when calcium carbonate-rich water flowed through the pores and deposited calcite. The relative proportions of quartz and calcite cement varied depending on the local conditions.

Grain X was now firmly bound to its neighbors. It could no longer be moved by water currents or by any other force short of significant tectonic activity or erosion. It was part of a solid rock—a sandstone that would remain relatively unchanged for millions of years.
